ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Geronimo

code.originalText: Establishing care at the clinic for poor sleep, nightmares and drinking at night: a trauma-informed history with the interpreter, PTSD, alcohol, depression and cognitive screening, liver tests, a recent fall, and his safety

text.paragraph: Establishing care at the clinic for poor sleep, nightmares and drinking at night: a trauma-informed history with the interpreter, PTSD, alcohol, depression and cognitive screening, liver tests, a recent fall, and his safety [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He wants to sleep through the night without the old battles and the dead coming back to him. [S]
He does not want whisky to rule his nights, and he does not want to fall again. [S]
He wants care that respects who he is, his people and his own ways of healing. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: By his own account he was born in June 1829 in No-doyohn Cañon, in the country around the headwaters of the Gila River; the National Park Service places his birth on the Gila River in New Mexico, not far from the Gila Cliff Dwellings, and the Oklahoma Historical Society gives the 1820s, perhaps near present Clifton, Arizona. [D]

His Apache birth name is written Goyakla by the National Park Service and Goyahkla by the Oklahoma Historical Society, meaning one who yawns; he belonged to the Bedonkohe (Bedonkehe) band of the Chiricahua Apache and, in the Park Service's words, was not a chief but a medicine man. [D]
He prayed to Usen, the Apache word for God, and believed throughout his life that Usen had told him he would never die in battle or by a gun. [D]

While his band was trading at a Mexican town the Apaches called Kas-ki-yeh, Mexican troops attacked the camp; when he returned he found that his aged mother, his young wife and his three small children were among the dead. His own account dates this to the summer of 1858; the National Archives gives 1851 and the Oklahoma Historical Society 1850. [D]

In his own words, that night he stood alone by the river, did not vote in the council, had no weapon and hardly wished to fight, and 'had no purpose left'; on the march home he did not eat and spoke to no one. At home he burned his family's belongings, vowed vengeance, and wrote that he was never again contented in his quiet home. [D]

He listed eight wounds received in his wars with Mexican forces, among them a gunshot to the right leg above the knee (the bullet still carried), a gunshot through the left forearm, a saber wound below the right knee, a blow to the top of the head with a musket butt that knocked him senseless, a shot just below the outer corner of the left eye, and shots in the left side and the back. [D]

His final surrender was in Skeleton Canyon in southern Arizona in the summer of 1886 (September 1886, by the Oklahoma Historical Society). The promise that the men would see their families in Florida was not kept: he and his warriors were held at Fort Pickens, at hard labor sawing logs, and did not see their families until May 1887. [D]

As prisoners of war the Chiricahua Apache were held in Florida, then at Mount Vernon in Alabama, and from 1894 at Fort Sill; many died of malaria in Florida, many children died of tuberculosis in Alabama, and only 119 remained when they were moved to Oklahoma. In his words, so many of his people died in Alabama that he let one of his wives go to the Mescalero Agency. [D]

At Fort Sill he was still held as a prisoner of war; the Apaches lived in houses the government built, raised cattle and farmed, and he was relieved from assigned labor because of his age but worked to help his people. He was held as a prisoner of war for the last 23 years of his life. [D]

He was allowed to leave Fort Sill under guard to appear at national expositions in Omaha (1898), Buffalo (1901) and St. Louis (1904), and he rode in a presidential inauguration parade in 1905, where he asked to be allowed to return to the Southwest with his people and was refused. [D]

In 1905 and 1906, with permission from the President and the officers at Fort Sill, he told his life story to S. M. Barrett through the interpreter Asa Deklugie (also written Daklugie), on condition that Barrett write what he had spoken; it was published in 1906 as Geronimo's Story of His Life. [D]
In his autobiography he said that since he had been a prisoner of war he had twice been arrested and placed in the guardhouse for drinking whisky. [D]

He described further losses and separations in his family during captivity: a wife who left for Mescalero with their two small children, the death of another wife, and a marriage in December 1905 that soon ended in separation. [D]
The project roster lists post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic grief as his anchor conditions; no historical source read makes either diagnosis. [R]

Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Eight wounds in wars with Mexican forces, including gunshot wounds of the right thigh (bullet retained), left forearm, left side and back, a saber wound below the right knee, and a glancing shot below the left eye
Blow to the top of the head with a musket butt, with loss of consciousness; no lasting effect recorded
Killing of his mother, wife and three children by Mexican troops, and his grief afterwards in his own words
Prisoner of war since 1886: hard labor at Fort Pickens apart from his family, then Alabama, where many of his people died of disease, and Fort Sill
Twice jailed in the guardhouse for drinking whisky as a prisoner of war, by his own account

tr.td: Killed by Mexican troops in an attack on the camp; not a medical cause of death
Three young children killed in the same attack

list.item: Chiricahua Apache of the Bedonkohe band; an elder respected by his people; lives alone in a small house on the military reservation near Fort Sill, where his people have been held by the federal government since they were brought there; cannot travel or return to his homeland without permission; keeps horses and cattle and works when he wishes [S]

Speaks Chiricahua Apache as his first language, with Spanish and some English; does not read English; chose to have the clinic's Apache-speaking interpreter at every visit; asked to be called Geronimo [S]

Lost his mother, his wife and his three children in an attack by soldiers when he was young; fought for decades; surrendered on promises that were not kept; was held at hard labor apart from his family; and has seen many of his people die in captivity. He spoke of these events briefly and in his own way, and chose what to share [S]

Alcohol: whisky most evenings for the past year, about four to six drinks, more on the nights the memories come; obtained in town; no withdrawal seizures or hallucinations when he has gone without; does not use commercial tobacco (ceremonial use not asked about); no other drugs [S]

Traditional healing: he prays in his own way and has his own ways of healing; he will decide whether and how they are part of his care; the clinic offered access through its traditional medicine program and asked nothing further [S]

Strengths and supports: his standing among his people, his faith, his work with horses and cattle, his skill in telling his own story, a long record of endurance, and clear views about what he wants [S]
No firearm or other weapon in his house; he keeps a knife for work with the cattle [S]

tr.td: Thiamine 100 mg oral tablet, one tablet daily

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, oriented, dignified and watchful; speech measured, through the interpreter; mood tired and heavy; affect restricted, warmer when speaking of his horses; startles at a door closing; no psychotic symptoms; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone; judgment and insight good. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

code.displayName: Physical findings of General status Narrative

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent in daily activities; rides and walks without a device; Timed Up and Go 13 seconds; one fall in the past month at night after drinking. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 2026-07-08; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Alert, oriented, dignified and watchful; speech measured, through the interpreter; mood tired and heavy; affect restricted, warmer when speaking of his horses; startles at a door closing; no psychotic symptoms; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone; judgment and insight good. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Structured safety assessment: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent, access to means reviewed: yes. Outpatient care with close follow-up. Risk factors reviewed without detail: post-traumatic stress, moderate alcohol use disorder, depressive symptoms, older age, living alone, a recent fall and many losses. He has no firearm; medicines are dispensed in small amounts. A written safety plan was made with him in his own words through the interpreter, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988, with interpreter services) and the clinic's number were written on a card he carries. Safety is reviewed at every visit. [S]

tr.td: Poor sleep for many years with nightmares and unwanted memories of past violence, worse over the past year; drinks at night to sleep; cause to be assessed

S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to the documented killing of his family and his years of war; resolved into the diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder at the consultation. Not a claim about his real sleep.

Alcohol use disorder, moderate (four DSM-5-TR criteria): drinking at night to sleep, more than intended, unable to cut down, and a fall walking home after drinking; AUDIT 19; liver tests show the pattern of heavy drinking
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis anchored to his own statement that he was twice jailed for drinking whisky as a prisoner of war; not a claim about his real drinking.
A fall in the past month while walking home at night after drinking: bruised left hip, no fracture on examination; Timed Up and Go 13 seconds
S — Synthetic fall-risk finding; it is not his documented last fall, which is history after the episode.

list.item: Poor sleep for many years with nightmares and unwanted memories of past violence, worse over the past year; drinks at night to sleep; cause to be assessed: active, confirmed [S]

Alcohol use disorder, moderate (four DSM-5-TR criteria): drinking at night to sleep, more than intended, unable to cut down, and a fall walking home after drinking; AUDIT 19; liver tests show the pattern of heavy drinking: active, confirmed [S]
A fall in the past month while walking home at night after drinking: bruised left hip, no fracture on examination; Timed Up and Go 13 seconds: active, confirmed [S]

Trauma-informed, culturally safe care: ask how he wishes to be addressed and what matters to him, the Apache interpreter at every visit, time and plain explanations, consent before each question about the past and each examination, no demand to retell the killings or name the dead, and his history shared only as he chooses. Guideline: Trauma-Informed Care in Behavioral Health Services (Treatment Improvement Protocol 57) (2014); Special General Memorandum 94-08: Statement of Policy for the Traditional Cultural Advocacy Program (1994) [S]

Psychiatry consultation at the clinic's visiting session to confirm the diagnosis with a structured interview, weigh grief against prolonged grief disorder, and advise on therapy and medicines. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Management of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Acute Stress Disorder (2023); Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in Adults (2017) [S]

PTSD screening and tracking: PC-PTSD-5 and PCL-5 at intake, a CAPS-5 interview to confirm, and the PCL-5 at each visit. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Management of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Acute Stress Disorder (2023) [S]

Alcohol: brief counseling with his own goals, DSM-5-TR criteria, PEth explained as part of care, thiamine, and liver and kidney tests before medicine; no withdrawal medicine needed (no past withdrawal seizures or delirium). Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); The Healthcare Professional's Core Resource on Alcohol (2026); Unhealthy Alcohol Use in Adolescents and Adults: Screening and Behavioral Counseling Interventions (2018) [S]

Safety: a structured safety assessment at intake, a written safety plan in his own words, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, small medicine supplies, and safety review at every visit. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]

Falls: Timed Up and Go at visits, orthostatic blood pressure, no drinking before riding or walking out at night, a light on the path to his house, and an exercise program for strength and balance. Guideline: Falls Prevention in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Interventions (2024) [S]

Traditional healing offered alongside clinic care at his choice, through the clinic's traditional medicine program, with nothing asked about his beliefs. Guideline: Special General Memorandum 94-08: Statement of Policy for the Traditional Cultural Advocacy Program (1994) [S]

Vaccines due at his age: pneumococcal conjugate, high-dose influenza, RSV, recombinant zoster and Tdap, at the wellness visit and the following visit. Guideline: Adult Immunization Schedule by Age (2026) [S]
Referral to psychiatry (trauma and ptsd), Dominic Achebe-Varga, MD, ordered 2026-07-08 [S]
